entries.name: Holmwood Capital Advisors, LLC, and Holmwood Capital, LLC v. HC Government Realty Holdings, L.P., et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Defendants' argument that the Termination Fee Estimate properly reduced Stockholders' Equity, and that reading "other non-cash items" in Adjustment One to include it would make Adjustment Two surplusage: rejected. The Estimate is a non-cash item that impacted GAAP stockholders' equity. Adjustment Two still has work to do for non-cash items GAAP would not permit HC REIT to record (e.g., internally generated goodwill, which Plaintiffs identified).

Defendants' argument that "builds" means "maintains," so the 3.0x multiplier is lost if Stockholders' Equity later falls below $35 million: rejected. "Builds" carries no temporal limitation, the parties imposed temporal limits elsewhere in the agreement (fn. 162), and the Court will not add omitted terms.

Defendants' argument that dividends were improperly added back to Stockholders' Equity: the Court agreed that "retained earnings" plainly excludes dividends, but held the argument waived. HC REIT knew of the deviation and delivered its final Termination Fee calculation on March 31, 2020 adding back dividends.

Defendants' argument that the Contributed Properties were overvalued by about $3.2 million: waived for the same reason. Alternatively rejected on the merits, assuming without deciding that the Court may second-guess the valuation. Scott's appraisal contained obvious errors, and its $2 million defeasance deduction would be a windfall because title later passed free and clear and no defeasance fee was paid.

Plaintiffs' argument that Section 10(f) lets HCA choose the form of Termination Fee Securities, and that Section 6(e)(ii) requires mutual consent before paying Acquisition Fees in common stock: rejected. Contra proferentem was applied against the Founder-drafted instrument, and Stanton's self-interested testimony was the only extrinsic evidence.

Plaintiffs' argument that Side Letter § 1 requires HCA to repay only reimbursements it actually received: rejected. The ambiguity was construed against Plaintiffs, so HCA must pay all O&O Expenses above the 15% cap.

Plaintiffs' argument that Holmwood could not have breached the Contribution Agreement because it had no obligation to procure lien releases before closing: rejected as conflating obligations. The separate No-Default Representation proved false.

Plaintiffs' argument that Contribution Agreement § 6.A allocates consent costs to Holdings, so Defendants suffered no damages: rejected. Section 6.A applies only to consents Holmwood procured before closing, and Holmwood procured none.

Plaintiffs' argument that HCA is owed Acquisition Fees for the Disputed Acquisitions because Defendants prevented performance through the Amended Investment Guidelines: rejected. Nothing prevented HCA from proposing acquisitions to the Board.

Plaintiffs' argument that the Shortfall Amounts were loans payable on demand at 8% interest (12% per internal Holmwood documents): not proven. Only Stanton's self-serving testimony supported the existence of a loan agreement.

summary.brief_summary: After a three-day trial, Vice Chancellor David resolved claims by HCA and Holmwood against HC REIT and Holdings over the Termination Fee and related fees, together with counterclaims for breach of the Management and Contribution Agreements and unjust enrichment. The Court held that the accrued Termination Fee Estimate must be added back to Stockholders' Equity, that the Side Letter's "builds" test is a high-water mark, and that HC REIT waived its belated dividend and overvaluation adjustments by delivering its final fee calculation without them. Applying contra proferentem because the Founders drafted the instruments for a vehicle they intended to market to investors, the Court construed the ambiguous payment-form and O&O provisions against Plaintiffs. It also held Holmwood liable for $517,463.35 for breaching its no-default representation by transferring the CMBS profits interest without lender consent.
summary.core_legal_issue: Following trial on cross-claims arising from HC REIT's non-renewal of HCA's Management Agreement, the principal questions were: (1) whether an accrued GAAP liability for the estimated Termination Fee had to be added back to "Stockholders' Equity" as an "other non-cash item[]"; (2) whether the Side Letter's requirement that HC REIT "build" $35 million of Stockholders' Equity sets a high-water mark or a test at termination; and (3) related disputes over the form of fee securities, O&O Expense repayment, undocumented "loans," and Holmwood's breach of a no-default representation by contributing the CMBS Properties' profits interest without lender consent.
summary.disposition: judgment in part for each side
summary.holding: Mixed judgment after trial. Termination Fee (Complaint Count I): the Termination Fee Estimate is an "other non-cash item[]" under Adjustment One and must be added back to Stockholders' Equity. Defendants waived their dividend and Contributed Properties challenges by delivering the March 31, 2020 calculation without them, and the overvaluation claim also fails on the merits (assuming without deciding the Court may revisit the valuation). "Builds" means achieves, so the 3.0x multiplier applies "[i]f Stockholders' Equity equaled or exceeded $35 million at any time prior to the Termination Date." Asset Management Fees must be recalculated on that basis and include the 24-month period ending March 31, 2020 (fn. 165). Plaintiffs did not prove that accrued Acquisition Fees went unpaid, because recording the shares with the transfer agent was not shown to fall short of payment. HCA earned no Acquisition Fees for the Disputed Acquisitions because it rendered no services and was not prevented from performing. Fn. 117 notes an analogous "AMF Accrual Estimate" add-back that neither party briefed. Form of payment: applying contra proferentem against the Founder-drafted Management Agreement, HC REIT could pay both the Termination Fee and the Acquisition Fees in common stock. Shortfall Amounts (Complaint Count III): no loan contract was proven, but the parties intended repayment; they must meet and confer on a repayment proposal. O&O Expenses: HCA must bear all O&O Expenses above the 15% cap ($723,932 excess). The record does not show whether HCA paid less than that amount, so the parties must meet and confer and, if necessary, submit payment documentation; that answer determines whether HC REIT's dividend and distribution offset was proper (fn. 206). Counterclaim Count I (duplicative property management fees and $7,500 in undocumented reimbursements): not proven; judgment for HCA. Counterclaim Count II: Holmwood breached the No-Default Representation; Defendants recover $517,463.35. The Bring-Down Representations breach yielded no proven additional damages. Counterclaim Count III (unjust enrichment): judgment for Plaintiffs. The parties must meet and confer in good faith to prepare a revised Termination Fee calculation jointly, and to submit a proposed form of order implementing the rulings.
key_facts_and_concessions: When CFO Piscetelli calculated Q3 2019 Asset Management Fees, she began treating the $1,750,000 Termination Fee Estimate (accrued under GAAP and reported in the Form 1-SA) as a liability. This cut Q2 2019 Stockholders' Equity from $37,133,134 to $34,904,007, below the Side Letter's $35 million threshold. HC REIT's March 31, 2020 Termination Fee of $1,645,453 used a 1.5x multiplier.
The parties agree the Termination Fee Estimate does not fall within Adjustment Two, which requires Board approval (fn. 126).

On July 12, 2019, Post (HCA's then-CFO) told Piscetelli that "dividends and distributions" were "excluded from common stock." Piscetelli said she might "adjust, if necessary" but never did. HC REIT's final March 31, 2020 Termination Fee calculation added back dividends, and HC REIT first raised the issue in a June 18, 2025 expert report.
Plaintiffs do not argue that adding back dividends was proper under the Management Agreement (fn. 149).

The Founders controlled HCA, HC REIT and Holdings when the Management Agreement was signed and expected HC REIT to be marketed to outside investors. HC REIT issued a preliminary offering circular within months.

Holmwood did not obtain consent from the CMBS lender before the Exchange Transaction. LNR, the servicer, issued a notice of default on November 16, 2022, and HC REIT spent $517,463.35 obtaining a Consent and Loan Modification Agreement on March 27, 2023.
At deposition, Stanton conceded that HCA "did not provide those services" for the three Disputed Acquisitions (fn. 177).

Holmwood transferred $408,514 in Shortfall Amounts to HC REIT without signed contracts. HC REIT does not deny receipt, its Form 1-K acknowledged the payable, and the parties agree the amounts were not a gift.
summary.practical_takeaway: A party that delivers a final contractual fee calculation after being told how its inputs deviate from the contract risks waiving later challenges to those inputs, so objections should be raised before the calculation is tendered. Founder-affiliated managers of vehicles intended for outside investors should draft fee-mechanics provisions unambiguously, because the Court will construe ambiguities against them even when the same founders sat on both sides.
summary.standard_of_review: Post-trial; each claimant and counterclaimant had to prove every element, including damages, by a preponderance of the evidence. Contracts were read under Delaware's objective theory and plain meaning. Ambiguous provisions (held ambiguous on summary judgment) were construed by contra proferentem rather than by extrinsic evidence.

entries.name: Kevin Leiske, et al. v. Robert Gregory Kidd, et al.

arguments_rejected_or_waived: Rollo's January 29 contention that defendants' counsel should have met and conferred before raising the GenAI errors with the Court: rejected. It misstates the purpose of the meet-and-confer requirement; there is nothing to negotiate when false citations or fabricated quotations are presented to a tribunal, and opposing counsel was fully justified in going directly to the Court.

Rollo's insistence that the cited authorities "are real" and "support the arguments advanced": rejected. Real cases and propositions arguably consistent with general law do not excuse fabricated quotations or mischaracterized holdings. Once errors are detected, counsel must review the authorities and correct them; removing quotation marks while leaving a fabricated legal synthesis in place is not enough.

Rollo's January 28 attribution of the errors to a paralegal's cite-check oversight: rejected. The Rule 11 inquiry and the duty of candor are personal and nondelegable, so a signing senior attorney cannot disclaim responsibility for unverified GenAI output. Rollo later disavowed blaming others.

Defendants' August 4, 2026 request (letter from M. DiBianca) for leave to present billing records and information about plaintiffs' counsel's time records: denied (fn. 36). Fees are unavailable under Rule 11(c)(4) because the inquiry was initiated sua sponte rather than on motion. The Court credited the sworn affidavits, so probing billing discrepancies would serve no useful purpose.

authorities_cited.proposition: A signer certifies after reasonable inquiry that legal contentions are warranted by existing law; presenting unverified GenAI output, including fake quotations or fabricated legal synthesis, violates the rule.
A firm must be held jointly responsible for its lawyers' violations absent exceptional circumstances; the Court may sanction any attorney who violated Rule 11(b) or is responsible for the violation.
A sanction must be limited to what suffices to deter; attorneys' fees are unavailable in a sua sponte Rule 11 proceeding.

authorities_cited.authority: Del. Lawyers' Rules of Prof. Conduct R. 5.1(a)
authorities_cited.proposition: Firm leadership must make reasonable efforts to have measures giving reasonable assurance of compliance; used as guidance on whether to relieve a firm of joint Rule 11 responsibility.

authorities_cited.authority: ABA Comm. on Ethics & Prof. Resp., Formal Op. 512 (2024)
authorities_cited.proposition: Managerial lawyers should set clear GenAI policies and supervisory lawyers should ensure compliance; a lawyer may not delegate professional judgment to GenAI and must verify work product before filing.

authorities_cited.authority: Johnson v. Dunn, 792 F. Supp. 3d 1241 (N.D. Ala. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: A firm that warned of hallucination risks and required verification is not sanctioned for a partner's GenAI misuse; no sanctions discount because real authorities support the bogus citations' propositions; sanctions aim at deterrence and vindicating judicial authority.

authorities_cited.authority: Mata v. Avianca, Inc., 678 F. Supp. 3d 443 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)
authorities_cited.proposition: A fake opinion is not "existing law"; Rule 11 obligations continue when later advocating a filing; a fine serves deterrence rather than punishment or compensation; fees are unavailable sua sponte; additional mandatory CLE is redundant where training already exists.

authorities_cited.authority: Hill v. Workday, Inc., 2026 WL 1146289 (N.D. Cal. Apr. 28, 2026)
authorities_cited.proposition: No separate sanctions hearing is needed when counsel can respond in writing; the duty to check filings is nondelegable to other attorneys or technology; upon detection counsel must personally review and correct; a sanctioned partner must pay personally.

authorities_cited.proposition: Fabricated quotations attributed to real cases and misstated law violate Rule 11(b); the reasonable-inquiry duty is nondelegable; downplaying errors as mostly human-drafted is rejected.

authorities_cited.authority: Pavelic & LeFlore v. Marvel Ent. Grp., 493 U.S. 120 (1989)
authorities_cited.proposition: Rule 11 brings home to the individual signer a personal, nondelegable responsibility.

authorities_cited.authority: Del. Lawyers' Rules of Prof. Conduct R. 3.3(a)(1), 5.3
authorities_cited.proposition: Rule 11's certification reinforces the duty of candor to the tribunal and the duty to supervise nonlawyer assistants.

authorities_cited.proposition: Comparator for the monetary penalty: $3,000 fines on attorneys who submitted AI-hallucinated authorities and deflected responsibility.

authorities_cited.authority: In re Kenney, 422 So. 3d 905 (La. Ct. App. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Sanctions affirmed where counsel relied on paralegals and did not independently verify AI-generated authorities.

authorities_cited.proposition: No filing should contain citations the responsible attorney has not personally read and verified.

authorities_cited.proposition: An attorney's signature is a certification to the tribunal.

authorities_cited.proposition: Deterrence is Rule 11's central purpose.

authorities_cited.authority: Jimenez-Fogarty v. Fogarty, 831 F. Supp. 3d 253 (S.D.N.Y. 2026); Wadsworth v. Walmart Inc., 348 F.R.D. 489 (D. Wyo. 2025); Mattox v. Prod. Innovations Rsch., LLC, 807 F. Supp. 3d 1341 (E.D. Okla. 2025); Benjamin v. Costco Wholesale Corp., 779 F. Supp. 3d 341 (E.D.N.Y. 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: Range of monetary penalties ($1,000 to $3,000) in comparable GenAI and Rule 11 proceedings.

authorities_cited.authority: Wilson v. Kipp Texas, Inc., 2025 WL 3030444 (N.D. Tex. Oct. 29, 2025)
authorities_cited.proposition: GenAI fabricates plausible verbatim quotations.

summary.brief_summary: After the merits of an advancement dispute were resolved, Vice Chancellor Will issued a sua sponte Order to Show Cause to plaintiffs' signing counsel, Richard Rollo, and his firm, RLF, over an answering brief containing GenAI-fabricated quotations and mischaracterized authorities. The corrected version of that brief stripped the quotation marks but kept the inaccurate case descriptions. The Court held that RLF's pre-existing GenAI policy, verification requirements and training were exceptional circumstances excusing the firm from joint responsibility. It held that Rollo violated Rule 11(b)(2) because the reasonable-inquiry duty is nondelegable, real cases and arguably correct propositions do not excuse fabricated quotations or holdings, and opposing counsel need not meet and confer before reporting fabrications. Rollo was fined $2,500, payable personally.
summary.core_legal_issue: Whether Court of Chancery Rule 11 sanctions should issue, on a sua sponte Order to Show Cause, against the partner who signed an answering brief containing GenAI-fabricated quotations and mischaracterized authorities, and against his firm, Richards, Layton & Finger, P.A. ("RLF"); and whether RLF's GenAI policies and training were "exceptional circumstances" relieving it of joint responsibility under Rule 11(c)(1).
summary.holding: RLF is released from the proceeding without sanction. The Court found that RLF showed exceptional circumstances under Rule 11(c)(1): its pre-filing ban on unapproved tools, its GenAI working group, its Board-adopted verification policy and its accredited mandatory training were reasonable efforts to prevent GenAI misuse, so it should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls. Rollo violated Rule 11(b)(2). He introduced unverified GenAI output into the brief, relied on others for cite-checking although the inquiry duty is personal and nondelegable, and, after the errors were flagged, removed quotation marks while leaving mischaracterized holdings in place. The Court treated his initial blame-shifting and retained mischaracterizations as aggravating. It weighed against them his sworn acceptance of full responsibility, his sincere contrition and his distinguished practice before the Court. Additional mandatory CLE would be redundant given his completed GenAI ethics CLE and his training role. Citing the range of fines in similar sua sponte proceedings, the Court fined Rollo $2,500 under Rule 11. Because the verification duty is nondelegable, he must pay it personally to the Court within 14 days and file an affidavit confirming payment. Defendants' request to present billing records was denied (fn. 36) because fees are unavailable in a sua sponte Rule 11 proceeding. The matter was resolved on the papers without an evidentiary hearing.
key_facts_and_concessions: Plaintiffs' lead counsel, Richard Rollo, Esq., signed the January 22, 2026 answering brief opposing exceptions to a Magistrate in Chancery's final report on advancement. Defendants' reply identified fabricated quotations, inaccurate citations, and hallucinated legal propositions in it.

As Chair of RLF's AI Subcommittee, Rollo was leading a pilot evaluation of Perplexity Enterprise, a tool not approved for general firm use. He used it to help draft and condense arguments, which introduced fabricated quotations, flawed citations, and a mischaracterized case holding.
Rollo delegated cite-checking to a junior attorney and a paralegal. He filed the brief without personally verifying the authorities or checking the citations and quotations after that review.

Rollo's January 28 letter attributed the errors to an oversight in a paralegal's cite-check. The corrected brief he filed removed the quotation marks around the nonexistent quotes but retained the inaccurate descriptions of the underlying cases.
Rollo's January 29 letter faulted defendants' counsel for not meeting and conferring before alerting the Court, and insisted the cited authorities "are real" and "support the arguments advanced."

RLF's safeguards were in place before the brief was filed: it barred unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023 and formed a GenAI working group in 2024. Its Board adopted a GenAI policy in July 2025 requiring an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output. Its CLE-accredited ethics training on GenAI had been completed by over 200 RLF employees by January 2026.

In his affidavit, Rollo acknowledged the Rule 11 violation under oath, accepted full responsibility, disavowed any suggestion that others were to blame, and expressed sincere contrition. He has completed multiple CLE courses on GenAI ethics and leads internal training efforts.

On February 2, 2026, the Court overruled the exceptions and affirmed the Magistrate's final report on the merits, retaining jurisdiction over the GenAI errors. It entered the Order to Show Cause on July 1, 2026 under Rule 11(c) and its inherent authority.
summary.practical_takeaway: The signing attorney must personally confirm that every quotation and characterization drawn from GenAI-assisted drafting matches the actual authority. Once errors are flagged, rewrite or withdraw every inaccurate proposition rather than merely stripping quotation marks, and do not deflect blame to cite-checkers or opposing counsel. A firm can avoid joint Rule 11 responsibility by having a written GenAI policy requiring lawyer verification, together with enforced training, in place before the filing.
summary.standard_of_review: Ct. Ch. R. 11(b)(2) (legal contentions must be warranted by existing law after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances); Ct. Ch. R. 11(c)(1) (firm jointly responsible absent exceptional circumstances); Ct. Ch. R. 11(c)(4) (sanction limited to what suffices to deter). Decided on the affidavits without a separate evidentiary hearing.
